what: Batch inference sends thousands of model requests as one job that runs in the background. You get results later, usually within hours, at about half the normal price.
like: Like dropping a big bag of laundry at the service wash: cheaper than the express counter, ready later, and every item comes back with its tag.
why: Half price on OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini batch APIs
Separate, larger limits, so bulk jobs never eat your live traffic quota
Perfect for overnight work: parsing millions of AI answers, evals, embedding backfills

steps.d: Each line is one full request plus your own unique id (custom_id on OpenAI and Anthropic, key on Gemini). Use a stable id like doc-123-v2.
Upload the file and create the job. The provider validates it, then queues it. Batch has its own rate limits, so live traffic is untouched.
The provider works through requests when it has room, within a 24 hour window. Many batches finish much sooner; Anthropic says most finish within an hour.
Poll the status every minute or so, or have OpenAI call your webhook when the batch completes. Then download the results file.
Results can come back in any order, so join each line to its input by custom_id, never by line number, and write to your store.
Some requests error or expire while others succeed. Collect just those ids and send them in a new, smaller batch.

choices.d: Split big jobs into chunks under the limits (50,000 on OpenAI, 100,000 on Anthropic, 2 GB file on Gemini). Smaller chunks finish sooner and retry more cheaply.
Make custom_id stable and meaningful (input id plus prompt version). Writing results as upserts by that id makes reruns safe.
Polling is simple and works everywhere. OpenAI webhooks push an event when a batch completes, which avoids a polling loop for many jobs.
Put the shared instructions first in every request. Anthropic says batch and cache discounts stack; use the 1 hour cache since batches can run past 5 minutes.
On your own GPUs, an engine like vLLM batches requests on the fly for high throughput. Worth it at steady huge volume with an open model.

instead.why: Normal live calls when a user is waiting for the answer
Your own queue and workers when you need minutes, not hours
Orchestrate the whole nightly pipeline around the batch jobs

breaks.d: Output order differs from input order, so answers land on the wrong rows.
breaks.see: Spot checks show answers that do not fit their inputs
breaks.fix: Always join on custom_id; reject duplicate ids before upload

breaks.d: A few requests error or expire, and the job is marked done anyway.
breaks.see: Row count in the store below the input count
breaks.fix: Read the error results, retry only those ids, alert on gaps

breaks.d: A huge batch is not finished inside the window; the rest is cancelled.
breaks.fix: Smaller chunks, start earlier, resubmit the expired ids

breaks.d: One wrong model name or field fails validation, or every line errors.
breaks.see: Batch failed at validating, or 100% errored results
breaks.fix: Send 10 lines as a test batch first, validate JSONL locally

breaks.d: A live feature waits on a batch that can take hours.
breaks.see: Users see spinners or stale data
breaks.fix: Live calls for users; batch only for offline work

say: Scoring last night's 2 million AI answers for brand mentions doesn't need to be live, so I'd run it through the batch API at half price.
I'd write one JSONL file per 50k requests, each with a stable custom_id, then poll or take a webhook and join results back by that id.
Some lines will error or expire, so the job collects those ids and resubmits just them, and our writes are upserts so reruns are safe.
Every request starts with the same instructions, so prompt caching with the 1 hour lifetime stacks with the batch discount.

followups.q: When would you not use a batch API?
followups.a: Anything a person is waiting for: chat, search answers, live agents. Results can take up to 24 hours. Also small jobs where the saving is tiny and a simple loop is easier.

followups.q: How do you handle partial failures?
followups.a: Each result has a type: succeeded, errored, canceled or expired. Anthropic does not bill the non-succeeded ones. Collect their custom_ids, fix the cause if it's an invalid request, and resubmit just those in a new batch.

followups.q: Batch API vs continuous batching in vLLM?
followups.a: A batch API is a product: cheaper, slower, async jobs. Continuous batching is a serving trick: the engine keeps the GPU full by swapping requests in and out every step. vLLM reports up to 24x the throughput of plain HF Transformers.

followups.q: How would you run an embedding backfill?
followups.a: Chunk the corpus, build JSONL embedding requests keyed by chunk id, submit in chunks under the limits, upsert vectors by id. OpenAI and Gemini both accept embeddings in batch.

today: All three big providers now offer batch at 50% off: OpenAI Batch, Anthropic Message Batches and Gemini Batch Mode, which also supports embeddings and context caching.

check.q: How do you match batch results to their inputs?
check.a: By the custom_id you set on each request
d: By line number in the output file
By the timestamp on each result
check.why: Results can come back in any order. The id is the only safe join key.

check.q: Which job is a good fit for a batch API?
check.a: Re-scoring last month's 2 million AI answers overnight
d: A live agent booking a meeting
check.why: Nobody is waiting, and it is big, so half price matters and hours are fine.

check.q: A batch ends with 3% expired requests. What next?
check.a: Resubmit only the expired ids in a new batch
d: Ignore them, they were billed anyway
Switch every request to live calls
check.why: Only the missing ones need work. Upserts by id keep the store clean.

check.q: Why use the 1 hour cache lifetime with batches?
check.a: Batches can run longer than 5 minutes, so the default cache may expire
d: It makes results come back in order
check.why: A longer lifetime keeps the shared prefix cached across the whole run.
